node.label: Linda Gordon
node.date_label: Heroes of Their Own Lives (1988) · Pitied But Not Entitled (1994) · The Great Arizona Orphan Abduction (1999)
node.description: Historian of gender, social policy and unequal power in American families. Gordon’s autobiographical account links her turn to women’s history with the women’s liberation movement. Her research on welfare and family violence treats domestic relations as public and political, while The Great Arizona Orphan Abduction reconstructs the interaction of race, family claims and local power through a tightly focused narrative.

named_group_routes.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.

named_group_routes.relationship: Governmentality: Foucault's 'Governmentality', Gordon, Burchell and Rose anthologised in his Class (1995); The Rule of Freedom 'develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography' (2003); governmentality as 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable', though prone to 'crypto-functionalism' (2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words: 'History and Governmentality' (2014, read in full), quoting Rose: governmentality 'concerns the ways in which those who would exercise rule have posed to themselves the question' of how to govern; 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable'; governmentality studies 'suffered also from a tendency to a sort of crypto-functionalism'; 'In developing the work of Foucault alongside the new materialism, I and my recent collaborator Chandra Mukerji begin from the assertion' that modern states are impersonal social formations. BJS 2010 (opening read) reprises Rose and Miller. Verso description of The Rule of Freedom (read): 'creatively and originally develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography'. Class (1995) contents: Foucault's 'Governmentality' (pp. 201–203), Gordon and Burchell, Donzelot, Rose. Koditschek (2014, read): The State of Freedom 'draws largely on the ideas of Michel Foucault'.

named_group_routes.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

named_group_routes.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 2025; text layer). The running heads give pp. 123–125 for the second to fourth pages, so the review runs pp. 122–125; the OJS record gives first page 121 and last page 124. Review pages are therefore not used as locators; quotations of the book carry Belshaw's references to the book. Passages used: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout'; 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305); census making 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26); 'a uniform enumeration would make a single Canadian population when in fact there were two' (book p. 98); 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'; criticisms: the Nova Scotian and New Brunswick systems grafted on 'as though they were unproblematic', no bibliography, and 'deadening jargon' in the introduction and conclusion.

sources.scope_note: Near-period (2002) review; the witness to the census book's wording.

The body of Wilson’s cited 1997 essay remains unread. The older Turner claim and its qualifications remain intact.
